1-1.description: Two black-and-white images: a portrait of George Cayley (top) and a replica glider in flight, with a fabric wing above an open boat-shaped carriage holding a pilot, and a cruciform tail (bottom).

1-2.description: Two black-and-white photographs: a portrait of Otto Lilienthal (top) and Lilienthal hanging beneath a glider in flight beside a hill, watched by a crowd (bottom).

1-3.description: Black-and-white portrait photograph of Octave Chanute, seated.

1-4.description: Black-and-white photograph of the Wright Flyer, a biplane made of wood and fabric, just above the ground, with a man standing to the right.

1-5.description: Black-and-white photograph of the Bleriot monoplane in flight just above a field, with a single wing above an open-frame fuselage.

1-6.description: Black-and-white photograph of the Junkers J-1 all-metal monoplane on the ground in front of a hangar, with a man standing beside it.

1-7.description: Black-and-white photograph of a Breguet 14 biplane on the ground, with two stacked wings braced by struts and wires.

1-8.description: Black-and-white aerial photograph of a Curtiss HS-2L flying boat on the water, with a boat-shaped hull, a biplane wing and military star insignia.

1-9.description: Photograph of a De Havilland Mosquito, a twin-engine propeller aircraft, parked on its main gear with wheel chocks.

1-10.description: Photograph of a white Cessna Citation Mustang light business jet in flight, with two engines mounted on the rear fuselage.

1-11.description: Four photographs: a Goodyear blimp (lighter-than-air, top left), a glider in flight (top right), a helicopter (rotorcraft, bottom right) and a high-wing airplane (bottom left).

1-12.description: Three photographs: a low-wing monoplane on a ramp (top), a blue and yellow biplane in flight (middle) and a black-and-white photo of a triplane with three stacked wings (bottom).

1-13.description: Labeled illustration of a high-wing airplane with its principal units: wings, powerplant, fuselage, stabilizers, flight controls (on the wings and tail) and landing gear.

1-14.description: Illustrations of the five stresses: A. Tension (hands pulling a bar apart); B. Compression (hands pushing the ends of a bar together); C. Torsion (hands twisting a bar); D. Shear (two plates pulled in opposite directions across a single fastener); E. Bending (the combination stress), a bent structural member with tension outside of the bend, compression inside of the bend, and shear along an imaginary line (dotted).

1-15.description: Labeled illustration of a welded tube truss fuselage frame with longerons, vertical web members and diagonal web members.

1-16.description: Labeled illustration of a monocoque structure: a tube of skin over formers, closed at the end by a bulkhead.

1-17.description: Labeled illustration of semimonocoque construction: skin over a framework of bulkheads, longerons and stringers.

1-18.description: Photograph of a metal gusset plate (marked by an arrow) riveted across a joint between structural tubes.

1-19.description: Top-view illustrations of six wing shapes: tapered leading edge with straight trailing edge; tapered leading and trailing edges; delta wing; sweptback wings; straight leading and trailing edges; straight leading edge with tapered trailing edge.

1-20.description: Front-view illustrations of six wing positions and shapes: low wing, dihedral (wings angled upward, with a dashed reference line), high wing, mid wing, gull wing and inverted gull.

1-21.description: Rear view of a twin-engine low-wing airplane in flight, with the left wing labeled on the left and the right wing on the right, as seen from the pilot's seat.

1-22.description: Front-view illustrations of wing bracing: full cantilever wings (no external bracing, two examples); semicantilever wings with struts (two examples); a wire braced biplane; and a high wing with long struts braced with jury struts.

1-23.description: Two labeled cutaway illustrations of a wing. Left: nose ribs and ribs between the front spar and rear spar. Right: skin over ribs and stringers.

1-24.description: Cutaway illustration of a wing built as a box beam, with the skin cut away to show box-shaped compartments formed by spars and ribs.

1-25.description: Illustrations of five wooden spar cross-sections labeled A to E: A, solid rectangular; B, solid with routed sides; C, hollow box; D, I-shaped; E, solid with a laminated section.

1-26.description: Illustrations of five metal spar shapes, including I-beams and channel sections, one with lightening holes in the web and one built from two channels back to back.

1-27.description: Labeled illustration of a truss spar: upper cap member and lower cap member joined by vertical tubes and diagonal tubes, with riveted gusset plates at the joints.

1-28.description: Labeled illustration of a plate web spar: upper spar cap, lower spar cap, a web with vertical stiffeners, and a rib attach angle.

1-29.description: Labeled illustration of a spar with caps along the top and bottom and a sine wave web (a corrugated web) between them.

1-30.description: Labeled illustration of a fail-safe spar: an upper spar cap and lower spar cap, an upper spar web and a lower spar web joined by a riveted splice, and rows of rivets.

1-31.description: Three illustrations of wooden wing ribs, labeled A to C: A, a truss rib of cap strips and diagonal braces; B, a truss rib with plywood gussets and a lightened trailing section; C, a plywood web rib with round lightening holes.

1-32.description: Labeled plan view of a wood wing structure: wing tip, leading edge strip, nose rib or false rib, front spar, rear spar, anti-drag wire or tie rod, drag wire or tie rod, wing rib or plain rib, wing butt rib (or compression rib or bulkhead rib), wing attach fittings, false spar or aileron spar, aileron and aileron hinge.

1-33.description: Photograph of the side of a low-wing aircraft, with the wing root fairing between the wing and fuselage outlined in yellow.

1-34.description: Labeled cutaway illustration of a removable metal wing tip: upper skin, access panel, leading edge outer skin, corrugated inner skin, louver, heat duct, reflector rod, wing cap, wing tip navigation light, and points of attachment to front and rear spar fittings (2 upper, 2 lower).

1-35.description: Cutaway illustration of a stressed skin wing section, with the skin cut away to show closely spaced ribs and stringers that carry load with the skin.

1-36.description: Cutaway illustration of a wing with part of the upper skin removed to show a sealed structure fuel tank (wet wing) built into the wing, with a filler opening on top.

1-37.description: Labeled cross-sections of honeycomb panels: A, constant thickness, a core between two skins of equal spacing; B, tapered core, skins converging to a point at one end.

1-38.description: Labeled illustration of the trailing edge area of a large jet wing, showing where sandwich panels are used: trailing edge sandwich panels (constant-thickness core), spoiler sandwich panels (tapered core, solid wedge), aileron tab sandwich panels (tapered core, phenolic wedge, and constant-thickness core), and a trailing edge wedge sandwich panel (tapered core, cord wedge). Also labeled: wing leading edge, outboard flap and inboard flap.

1-39.description: Labeled cutaway illustration of a wing leading edge: a honeycomb sandwich core between glass reinforced plastic skins, with wooden members spanwise and chordwise, and a metal member bonded to the sandwich and joined to the metal wing spar.

1-40.description: Photograph of a twin-engine airplane taking off with its gear retracting into the engine nacelles, with an inset close-up of a main wheel retracting into a nacelle.

1-41.description: Photograph of the firewall at the front of a yellow high-wing aircraft's fuselage with the engine removed, showing the metal firewall panel with fittings, above the nose gear.

1-42.description: Photograph of a horizontally opposed engine with its cowling removed, mounted on a tubular engine mount, with exhaust pipes below.

1-43.description: Illustration of the cowling for a horizontally opposed engine shown separated into its panels: top panels, side panels, the nose cowl around the propeller, and the spinner.

1-44.description: Illustration of orange peel cowling for a radial engine: four curved cowl panels hinged open around the engine opening, like the sections of a peeled orange.

1-45.description: Photograph of a turbofan engine nacelle on a transport aircraft with the cowling halves hinged open on each side of the engine, showing the fan at the front.

1-46.description: Labeled cutaway illustration of a tail cone: frames, bulkheads, longerons, stringers and skin, tapering toward the tail.

1-47.description: Labeled illustration of an empennage on the end of a fuselage: vertical stabilizer, rudder, horizontal stabilizer, elevator, and trim tabs on the rudder and elevator.

1-48.description: Labeled cutaway illustration of a vertical stabilizer structure: spars, ribs and stringers under the skin.

1-49.description: Illustration of an airplane with its three axes of rotation: the elevator controls pitch around the lateral axis (longitudinal stability); the rudder controls yaw around the vertical axis (directional stability); the ailerons control roll around the longitudinal axis (lateral stability). A table below summarizes them.
1-49.table:
| Primary Control Surface | Airplane Movement | Axes of Rotation | Type of Stability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aileron | Roll | Longitudinal | Lateral |
| Elevator/Stabilator | Pitch | Lateral | Longitudinal |
| Rudder | Yaw | Vertical | Directional |

1-50.description: Labeled side-view illustration of an aluminum control surface rib: the spar at the front, an aileron hinge-pin fitting, an actuating horn, and lightening holes in the rib.

1-51.description: Three photographs of aircraft that use composite control surfaces: a red and white Coast Guard helicopter in flight, a Boeing 787 airliner in front of a hangar with a crowd, and a low-wing single-engine airplane on grass.

1-52.description: Six cross-section illustrations of a wing trailing edge with an aileron (orange) behind it, each showing a different hinge point location close to the front of the aileron.

1-53.description: Four top-view illustrations of wing tips, each with the aileron (hatched) in a different position along the trailing edge near the tip.

1-54.description: Illustration of a high-wing airplane with one aileron deflected down (labeled down aileron) and the other deflected up (labeled up aileron), above a control yoke turned to one side.

1-55.description: Labeled illustration of a flight deck control linkage: control columns connected through torque tubes and bellcranks, with elevator cables, cables to the ailerons, stops, and a tether stop. A note reads: "Note pivots not on center of shaft".

1-56.description: Labeled illustration of a transport aircraft wing from above, showing an inboard aileron, an outboard aileron and several flight spoilers on the upper surface.

1-57.description: Photograph of a black flying-wing jet in flight, with the elevons along the trailing edges of both wings outlined and labeled.

1-58.description: Close-up photograph of the root of a horizontal stabilizer on a transport aircraft, with index marks on the fuselage beside the stabilizer leading edge.

1-59.description: Photograph of a V-tail airplane from behind, with one of the two ruddervators outlined and labeled.

1-60.description: Photograph of a red high-wing airplane on grass, with the flaperons along the wing trailing edge outlined and labeled.

1-61.table:
| Name | Location | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Flaps | Inboard trailing edge of wings | Extends the camber of the wing for greater lift and slower flight. Allows control at low speeds for short field takeoffs and landings. |
| Trim tabs | Trailing edge of primary flight control surfaces | Reduces the force needed to move a primary control surface. |
| Balance tabs | Trailing edge of primary flight control surfaces | Reduces the force needed to move a primary control surface. |
| Anti-balance tabs | Trailing edge of primary flight control surfaces | Increases feel and effectiveness of primary control surface. |
| Servo tabs | Trailing edge of primary flight control surfaces | Assists or provides the force for moving a primary flight control. |
| Spoilers | Upper and/or trailing edge of wing | Decreases (spoils) lift. Can augment aileron function. |
| Slats | Mid to outboard leading edge of wing | Extends the camber of the wing for greater lift and slower flight. Allows control at low speeds for short field takeoffs and landings. |
| Slots | Outer leading edge of wing forward of ailerons | Directs air over upper surface of wing during high angle of attack. Lowers stall speed and provides control during slow flight. |
| Leading edge flap | Inboard leading edge of wing | Extends the camber of the wing for greater lift and slower flight. Allows control at low speeds for short field takeoffs and landings. |

NOTE: An aircraft may possess none, one, or a combination of the above control surfaces.

1-62.description: Five photographs of aircraft with flaps extended: a low-wing airplane approaching to land, the view along an airliner wing with flaps lowered, a close-up of an extended flap, an airliner seen from below with flaps down, and a high-wing airplane seen from below with flaps down.

1-63.description: Cross-section illustrations of three flap types: A, plain flap (the rear part of the wing hinges down); B, split flap (only the lower surface hinges down); C, Fowler flap (the flap slides back and down, leaving a gap).

1-64.description: Cross-section illustration of a triple-slotted flap, shown retracted under the wing trailing edge and extended as three separate sections labeled fore flap, mid flap and aft flap, with slots between them.

1-65.description: Labeled cross-section of a Krueger-type leading edge flap: shown flap retracted inside the wing leading edge and (dashed) flap extended down and forward, with a hinge point, an actuator and a retractable nose.

1-66.description: Two photographs of a Krueger flap on a Boeing 737: a side view of the extended flap under the wing leading edge (left) and a front view of the leading edge beside the engine (right).

1-67.description: Photograph from below of a wing leading edge with a slat extended forward on its tracks, leaving a slot behind it.

1-68.description: Photograph of a transport aircraft wing upper surface during landing, with the spoiler panels raised.

1-69.table:
| Type | Direction of Motion (in relation to control surface) | Activation | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trim | Opposite | Set by pilot from cockpit. Uses independent linkage. | Statically balances the aircraft in flight. Allows "hands off" maintenance of flight condition. |
| Balance | Opposite | Moves when pilot moves control surface. Coupled to control surface linkage. | Aids pilot in overcoming the force needed to move the control surface. |
| Servo | Opposite | Directly linked to flight control input device. Can be primary or back-up means of control. | Aerodynamically positions control surfaces that require too much force to move manually. |
| Anti-balance or Anti-servo | Same | Directly linked to flight control input device. | Increases force needed by pilot to change flight control position. De-sensitizes flight controls. |
| Spring | Opposite | Located in line of direct linkage to servo tab. Spring assists when control forces become too high in high-speed flight. | Enables moving control surface when forces are high. Inactive during slow flight. |

1-70.description: Illustration of a vertical stabilizer and rudder with a small metal plate on the rudder trailing edge, labeled "Ground adjustable rudder trim".

1-71.description: Illustration of a fixed surface, a control surface and a tab, with airflow lines. The control surface is deflected down and the tab up, labeled "Tab geared to deflect proportionally to the control deflection, but in the opposite direction", with an arrow marked Lift.

1-72.description: Labeled illustration of a servo tab: a control stick is connected by a rod to the tab, and a free link joins the control surface at its hinge line.

1-73.description: Labeled illustration of a spring tab: a control stick connected through a free link to the tab, with a spring in a parallel linkage to the control surface.

1-74.description: Labeled cross-section of a wing and aileron with a balance panel: a hinged balance panel in a chamber ahead of the aileron, vent gaps above and below, a control tab on the aileron, and the hinge. Airflow lines show lower pressure under the wing acting through the vent gap on the balance panel.

1-75.description: Cross-section of a wing trailing edge and aileron, with the balance panel (red) inside a sealed chamber just ahead of the aileron hinge.

1-76.description: Photograph of the tail of a light airplane with a stabilator. The stabilator pivot point and an antiservo tab on its trailing edge are labeled, with arrows showing the tab moving in the same direction as the stabilator.

1-77.description: Photograph of a Boeing 737 in flight, with an arrow pointing to the winglet turned upward at the wing tip.

1-78.description: Close-up photograph of the upper surface of a wing with a small vortex generator, a thin blade standing up from the skin.

1-79.description: Photograph of the leading edge of a low wing with two unusual vortex generators, curved fins mounted on the upper surface.

1-80.description: Illustration of a swept-wing jet fighter, with an enlarged view of the wing showing a stall fence (red), a thin vertical plate running chordwise across the wing.

1-81.description: Two photographs from below of control surface gaps: an aileron gap seal along the wing (left) and a tab gap seal on a trailing edge surface (right).

1-82.description: Two photographs: a high-wing Cessna on a runway with fixed gear in wheel fairings (top), and a twin-engine airplane from below with its retractable gear extended (bottom).

1-83.description: Four photographs of aircraft without wheels: a helicopter on skids, a floatplane on water, a twin-engine airplane on skis on snow, and a red hot air balloon.

1-84.description: Photograph of a yellow amphibious water bomber in flight, with a boat-hull fuselage, floats under the wings and its wheels extended.

1-85.description: Photograph of a high-wing airplane on amphibious floats in a hangar, with small wheels extended below the floats.

1-86.description: Photograph of a high-wing airplane on grass with two main wheels forward and a tail wheel at the rear.

1-87.description: Two photographs of airplanes with tricycle gear: a high-wing airplane on a ramp (top) and a low-wing airplane in flight with gear extended (bottom).

1-88.description: Side-view outline of a light airplane fuselage with vertical lines at fuselage stations, each labeled: FS –97.0, FS –85.20, FS –80.00, FS –59.06, FS –48.50, FS –31.00, FS –16.25, FS 0.00, FS 20.20, FS 37.50, FS 58.75, FS 69.203, FS 89.25, FS 109.375, FS 132.00, FS 154.75, FS 177.50, FS 189.10, FS 200.70, FS 214.00, FS 224.00, FS 234.00 and FS 273.52. A horizontal line at the tail is marked WL 0.00.

1-89.description: Top view of a horizontal stabilizer with butt line stations on each side of the center: BL 16.00, BL 21.50, BL 23.25, BL 34.5, BL 47.27, BL 47.50, BL 61.50, BL 76.50, BL 86.56, BL 96.50 and BL 96.62.

1-90.description: Side view of a business jet with water lines marked: WL 7.55 and WL 9.55 near the ground line, WL 73.5, WL 79.5, WL 97.5 and WL 123.483.

1-91.description: Top-view diagram of a jet wing and nacelle with numbered stations: fuselage-wing station 0 at the centerline, wing stations from about 65.7 to 371 along the span, horizontal stabilizer stations from 15.2 to 122, nacelle stations (NAC centerline at BL 86.179, angled 2°), fuselage stations such as FS 625.30, FS 652.264 and FS 674.737, and winglet stations WGLTS 0.00 and WGLTS 49.89 (15° cant).

1-92.description: Illustration of a transport aircraft divided into numbered zones: Zone 100 lower half of fuselage, Zone 200 upper half of fuselage, Zone 300 empennage, Zone 400 engine nacelles, Zone 500 left wing, Zone 600 right wing, Zone 700 landing gear and landing gear doors, Zone 800 doors. Insets show subzones numbered within each zone (for example 111 to 146 in the lower fuselage and 311 to 351 in the empennage).

1-93.description: Labeled exploded illustration of a helicopter's major components: main rotor blades, main rotor hub assembly, pylon, fuselage, airframe, tail boom, stabilizer, tail rotor, tail skid, powerplant, transmission, and landing gear or skid.

1-94.description: Cutaway diagram of a turboshaft engine, color-coded for inlet air, compressor discharge air, combustion gases and exhaust gases. Sections from left: compression section (air inlet, compressor rotor), gearbox section (gear, output shaft, exhaust air outlet), turbine section (N2 rotor, stator, N1 rotor) and combustion section (combustion liner, fuel nozzle, igniter plug).

1-95.description: Labeled photograph of a four-blade hingeless main rotor head: main rotor hub, main rotor blades, blade pitch horns, pitch change links and main rotor mast.

1-96.description: Labeled illustration of a two-blade semirigid rotor head: blade grips, coning hinges, teetering hinge, blade pitch change horn, pitch link and swash plate.

1-97.description: Diagram of a rotor disk seen from above during forward flight at 100 knots. On the advancing side, blade tip speed plus helicopter speed gives a relative wind of 400 knots; on the retreating side, blade tip speed minus helicopter speed gives 200 knots. Arrows show blade rotation and the direction of flight.

1-98.description: Labeled illustration of a fully articulated rotor head: pitch change axis (feathering), pitch horn, flap hinge, drag hinge and damper, with one blade attached.

1-99.description: Photograph of a five-blade articulated main rotor head on top of a helicopter, viewed from the fuselage roof.

1-100.description: Top-view diagram of a helicopter: blade rotation produces torque in the opposite direction on the fuselage, shown as "Resultant torque from main rotor blades" pushing the tail one way, while tail rotor thrust pushes it the other way.

1-101.description: Photograph of the tail of a helicopter with a Fenestron, a fan enclosed in a round duct in the vertical fin.

1-102.description: Labeled illustration of a NOTAR helicopter: an air intake feeds a fan in the tail boom; air exits through slots along the boom and through a rotating nozzle at the tail. An inset shows the main rotor wake (downwash) and the air jet from the boom creating a sideways force labeled Lift.

1-103.description: Labeled illustration of collective control: raising the collective lever (with a throttle control on its end) moves linkages that raise the swash plate evenly, changing the pitch of all the rotor blades by the same amount.

1-104.description: Labeled illustration of cyclic control: moving the cyclic stick tilts the swash plate, which changes blade pitch around the disk. Insets show the rotor disk tilting for sideways flight (cyclic control stick moved sideways) and forward flight (cyclic control stick moved forward).
